question: What is actually moving in a copper wire when a lamp is lit?
options: Copper atoms
Free electrons, drifting along the wire
Protons leaving the battery
Light travelling inside the wire
explanation: In metals, some electrons are not tied to any atom. The battery pushes this crowd of free electrons so that it drifts round the loop. The copper atoms stay in place.

question: Two electrons are placed near each other. What do they do?
options: Pull together
Nothing at all
Push apart
Join into one particle
explanation: Like charges repel. Two negative charges push each other apart; a positive and a negative pull together.

question: Where do the electrons in a circuit come from?
options: They were already in the wire and the other parts; the battery only pushes them
The battery creates them when you switch on
They come from the air around the wire
The lamp makes them
explanation: A metal wire is always full of free electrons. The battery does not create any; it pushes the crowd that is already there.

question: You rub a balloon on your hair and the balloon becomes negatively charged. What happened?
options: The rubbing created new electrons on the balloon
Protons moved from the balloon to your hair
Some electrons moved from your hair to the balloon; no charge was created
The balloon lost all its electrons
explanation: Charge is never created or destroyed, only moved. A few electrons were scraped from the hair onto the balloon, so the balloon is negative and the hair is positive.

question: What is a coulomb?
options: A kind of particle, like the electron
The speed of electrons in a wire
A type of battery
A unit for an amount of charge: the charge of one fixed, very large crowd of electrons
explanation: Counting electrons one by one is hopeless, so we use the coulomb, a 'dozen' for charge, only immensely bigger. Phase 01 gives its exact size.

question: Each electron in a wire drifts very slowly. Why does a lamp still light the instant you close the switch?
options: The electrons speed up when the switch closes
The wire is already full of electrons, so the push reaches the lamp almost at once, like marbles in a full tube
The lamp stores light and releases it
The switch sends the electrons ahead of time
explanation: Push one marble into a full tube and one pops out of the far end at once. The push travels fast even though each marble barely moves.

question: Your phone battery is flat. Which statement is correct?
options: It has run out of stored energy; its electrons are all still there
It has run out of electrons
It has become strongly positive
It has lost all its charge to the charger cable
explanation: Charge stays balanced in the battery. What a flat battery lacks is the chemical energy it uses to push the electrons round.
